# How to view multiple websites at once
Source: https://tuliplot.com/blog/view-multiple-websites-at-once/
Published: 2026-08-02

Two situations send most people searching for this. You're comparing two things directly: two flight prices, two apartment listings, two drafts of the same document, and switching back and forth between tabs makes it hard to hold both in your head at once. Or you're watching one thing while working in another: a dashboard you want visible while you answer email, a video call running next to your notes. Either way, the goal is the same. You want to see two websites at the same time, not alternate between them all day.

There are five real ways to open two websites side by side, and this guide covers all five honestly, weaknesses included. Pick whichever fits how you actually work. You don't need to read past the one that solves your problem today.

## Can you see two websites at the same time in one browser?

Yes, in more than one way, and you likely already have what you need for the simplest version. Your operating system, your browser, and browser extensions can each put two sites on screen together, no new software required for the first two methods. Here's the short version of all five, in order from least to most permanent:

1. Your operating system's built-in split screen
2. Two separate browser windows, arranged by hand
3. A split-screen browser extension
4. A browser that tiles or splits tabs natively
5. A fixed dashboard grid, like TulipLot

The first four live inside whatever browser you already use. The fifth is a different kind of tool entirely, and it's worth understanding what it trades away before you get there.

## Method 1: your operating system's split screen

Windows has Snap: drag a window to either edge of the screen, or press the Windows key plus an arrow, and it fills exactly half, with a menu offering to fill the other half with a second window. macOS has Split View: hold down the green button in a window's top-left corner and choose a side, or drag one window to the edge while another sits ready to fill the rest. Both take about ten seconds and need nothing installed.

This is genuinely the fastest way to get two websites in view right now. It's built into the computer you already have, it costs nothing, and it works with any two windows, not just a browser, so the same trick handles a browser next to a spreadsheet just as easily as two browser windows.

The weakness is that it doesn't stick. Close the window, restart your computer, or just open a fresh browser session, and the split is gone. You're dragging to the edge again next time. And because a snapped window is still one whole browser window, if you've got other tabs open in it, one stray click on the wrong tab swaps out the site you were just comparing.

Who it suits: a quick, one-off comparison you won't need again tomorrow.

## Method 2: two browser windows side by side

This is the manual version of method 1. Instead of letting Snap or Split View decide the split, open a second browser window (not a new tab, a genuinely separate window: Ctrl+N or Cmd+N), drag it next to the first, and resize both by hand until you like the balance.

The upside over an automatic split is control. You can give one site 70% of the screen and the other 30%, stack them instead of placing them side by side, or spread them across two monitors if you have them. If you're comparing a wide spreadsheet against a narrow reference page, an even split rarely looks right, and this method fixes that.

The weakness is the same one as method 1, plus more of your own effort. You're rebuilding this every session, and now you're doing the resizing by hand instead of letting a keyboard shortcut do it for you. On a single small laptop screen, two full windows side by side often leaves each one too narrow to read comfortably, and you end up scrolling sideways on both.

Who it suits: anyone who wants exact control over the split and doesn't mind rebuilding it.

## Method 3: a split-screen browser extension

A category of browser extensions exists specifically to keep two sites inside one browser window, panes side by side, without needing two separate OS windows at all. Installed and set up once, some of these are genuinely useful: fewer windows to manage than method 2, and the split lives inside your normal browsing session instead of off to the side of it.

Here's the part worth knowing before you install one. Look closely at how a lot of these extensions actually work, and you'll notice many of them don't embed the second site inside the first pane at all. Instead they open it in a real, separate browser window, positioned and sized to look like a single split view. That's not a bug in the extension. It's because a real portion of the web refuses to be displayed inside another page under any circumstances, for a genuine security reason, and no extension can override that refusal. [Why some sites won't load in a dashboard](/guides/why-sites-wont-load) goes into exactly why that happens and what does and doesn't get around it, since the same rule shows up again later in this guide.

That's the honest weakness of this method: results depend heavily on which sites you're trying to split, not just which extension you pick. Some pairs of sites split cleanly. Others quietly fall back to a plain second window, which is functionally method 2 with an extra piece of software watching your browsing to make it happen. Worth weighing before you grant any extension that kind of access.

Who it suits: people happy staying inside one browser, comfortable granting an extension that access, whose particular sites happen to cooperate.

## Method 4: a browser that splits tabs natively

A handful of browsers build tab splitting straight into the browser itself, letting you drag one tab next to another so both are visible in the same window, no extension required. If you already use one of those browsers, this is close to free: the feature is just there, waiting.

The catch is right there in that sentence: it only helps if you're already using that browser, or willing to switch to one that has it. Switching your everyday browser is a bigger decision than installing an extension, mostly because of everything that comes along with it: saved passwords, bookmarks, other extensions, the dozens of sites that recognize you because you're already logged in there. None of that necessarily follows you cleanly to a new browser, and giving up your current setup just to get tab splitting is a real cost, not a minor one.

Who it suits: someone who already uses, or is genuinely happy to adopt, a browser that tiles tabs natively.

## Method 5: a fixed dashboard grid

Every method above shares one thing: you rebuild it. New session, new reboot, new week, and you're snapping, dragging, or re-splitting again, because none of the first four remember what you had open yesterday. That's fine for a comparison you'll only need once. It wears thin fast if it's the same two or three sites, every single day.

That's the gap TulipLot is built to close. It turns one browser tab into a fixed 3×2 grid, six cells, that looks exactly the same every time you open it. Put your project board top-center and your inbox top-left once, and they're still there tomorrow, and the week after, with nothing to rearrange each morning. Free covers five usable cells plus one ad cell in the bottom-right corner; Premium is $4 a month for all six cells with no ads. Free needs no credit card and has no time limit either way.

What actually happens when you add a site depends on the site, the same way it did in method 3, and it's worth being just as upfront about it here. Trello is a catalog example that loads live in the grid the moment you add it, nothing extra required. Notion and Hacker News are catalog examples that need a nudge first: the free TulipLot Companion, a Chrome extension you install once and then turn on for that specific site, after which they load live too. And Gmail, Outlook, and Google Calendar are catalog examples that never embed, Companion or not; each opens in its own browser tab as a one-click launcher instead, because their own protections run deeper than anything the Companion can adjust.

The tradeoff, stated plainly: methods 1 through 4 need nothing but what's already on your computer, and you can start using any of them in the next thirty seconds. Trying TulipLot needs nothing either — two cells load with no signup at [/try](/try) — though building out the full grid means creating a free account and spending a few minutes arranging it. What you get in exchange is that you stop spending those thirty seconds every single day.

## Which one should you use?

| Method | Best for | Setup | Sticks between sessions |
|---|---|---|---|
| OS split screen | A quick, one-off comparison | None | No |
| Two browser windows | Full manual control over the split | A few seconds, every time | No |
| Split-screen extension | Staying inside one browser window | One-time install | No |
| Tab-splitting browser | Anyone who already uses one | None, if you're already using it | No |
| Fixed dashboard grid | The same sites, day after day | A few minutes, once | Yes |

## Questions people ask

### Is there a website that shows multiple websites at once?

Not one that works for every site, no. Tools that try, TulipLot included, run into the same rule: a site can tell browsers not to display it inside another page, and browsers obey. Some sites allow it, some need a browser extension first, and a handful refuse outright no matter which tool is asking, because that choice belongs to the site itself, not to whatever's trying to display it. What you can find, and what's worth looking for, are tools that are upfront about which case each of your sites falls into instead of quietly showing a broken pane and leaving you to guess.

### Why won't some sites open side by side?

Because the site itself said no, not because anything you're using is broken. Browsers honor an instruction that some sites send back, blocking any other page from displaying them inside a frame, a genuine security measure meant to stop a trick called clickjacking, where a hidden frame tricks you into clicking something you never meant to. That decision happens before any split-screen extension or dashboard ever gets a say, which is why the same extension can work perfectly on one site and fail completely on the next. It's the site's own security choice, consistent across every tool, not a bug in whichever one you happen to be using.

### Does viewing multiple sites slow my computer down?

A little, but usually less than you'd expect. Two live webpages use more memory than one, the same way two browser tabs use more than a single tab does, but the difference between that and a single window is small on any computer bought in the last several years. What actually slows a machine down is a page that's heavy on its own, autoplaying video or a chat app refreshing nonstop, far more than the raw number of sites on screen. If one of your sites is like that, put it to sleep or close it when you're not using it, and everything else stays just as responsive.

Most people land on one of these five without ever needing the others, and any of them beats the alt-tab shuffle you started with. If your day involves the same handful of sites on repeat, [five ways to lay out a productive dashboard](/blog/dashboard-productivity-tips) is worth a look once you've picked your five (or six). And if a fixed grid sounds like the fit, [create a free account](/register) and see which of your own sites load live.

# What is a browser start page (and do you still need one)?
Source: https://tuliplot.com/blog/what-is-a-browser-start-page/
Published: 2026-08-02

"Start page," "home page," and "new tab page" get used like synonyms, and most people never notice they're three separate settings until one of them stops doing what they expect. All three are worth defining properly, because the differences explain a lot of what happened to the sites that used to live there, and what's worth using in their place today.

## Start page, home page, new tab: three different things

A start page is whatever loads when you launch the browser from fully closed, a cold start. It's controlled by your browser's startup setting, usually a choice between a blank page, one specific URL, or picking up your previous tabs right where you left off. In Chrome and Edge, that setting is launch-only: opening a fresh window while the browser is already running shows the New Tab page instead, not your configured start page.

A home page is what loads when you click the Home button, the small house icon some browsers still show next to the address bar. In Chrome and Edge, that's a separate setting from startup, one most people configure once and never touch again, and plenty of people have turned the Home button off entirely without realizing the setting underneath it is still there. Firefox draws the line differently: its single "Homepage and new windows" setting covers the Home button and the startup page together, so the two-setting split described here collapses into one there.

A new tab page is whatever appears every time you press Ctrl+T or Cmd+T. It's usually the browser's own screen of shortcuts and thumbnails, but it can be swapped out for something else, typically by installing an extension built for exactly that.

All three can point at the same URL, or three completely different ones. In Chrome and Edge, the settings are independent; in Firefox, the start page and home page are the same setting, and only the new tab page is separate. Either way, that overlap is exactly why the terms get confused with each other: once you've landed on one, it looks identical to whatever page happens to be showing in the tab. What changes is how you got there.

| Term | Opens when | Set in |
|---|---|---|
| Start page | The browser launches from a cold start | Startup settings |
| Home page | You click the Home button | Home-button settings (Chrome, Edge) |
| New tab page | You open a new tab | New Tab settings, often via an extension |

That's the shape in Chrome and Edge. Firefox combines the first two rows into one "Homepage and new windows" setting, so check there first if you're on Firefox and only one of these seems to exist.

## What start pages were for

Before "start page" meant a mostly blank new-tab screen, it meant something closer to a personal portal. Sites like iGoogle and Netvibes let you build one page out of small widgets: a weather box, a stock ticker, an inbox preview, a grid of RSS feeds pulling headlines in from wherever you pointed them. You set the result as your actual browser start page, and every time you opened the browser, that whole wall of information loaded before you did anything else.

The pitch made sense for its moment. Search engines were still catching up to being reliably good, so a page that pre-loaded the ten things you checked daily could genuinely save time over typing a query and picking through results. And most of what you wanted to check wasn't its own standalone app yet. Email lived in a browser tab, and so did nearly everything else worth checking: news, weather, sports scores, whatever your feeds pulled in. A portal start page wasn't competing against dedicated apps, because dedicated apps for most of that didn't really exist yet.

That's the part worth remembering before writing the whole category off as dated. The portal wasn't a workaround for anything. For a stretch of years, it was the most direct route to "everything in one place" that the web had on offer.

## Why the classics kept shutting down

iGoogle shut down in 2013. Netvibes has, since then, wound down the free version of its consumer product, the one regular people used without a company card attached to it.

Neither closure needs a conspiracy theory to explain it, and the same two shifts run underneath both. Search got good enough that pre-loading ten links and hoping one of them was useful stopped being faster than typing three words into a search box. And the things people actually wanted to check, email, calendars, project boards, chat, moved off feeds and static widgets and into dedicated apps with their own notifications, their own logins, their own reasons to be opened as a full tab instead of glanced at inside a box.

A page built for skimming headlines doesn't have much left to offer once the things you check are apps you actually use, not summaries you skim past. That's the pattern across the whole portal category, not just these two names specifically: build a page to aggregate a web that ran on RSS and static links, and it runs out of good answers once the web it was built for moves on without it.

## What people actually want now

Nobody's asking for that wall of widgets back, and it's worth being honest about why: feeds lost. RSS never fully disappeared, but it stopped being how most people track the things that matter to them day to day.

Ask most people what they actually check throughout the day and you get a short list, not a wall of links: email, a calendar, one or two chat tools, a project board, maybe a single news source they trust. Five or six things, at most, and every one of them is a full destination now, not a headline to glance at and move past. Nobody wants a summary of their inbox anymore. They want their inbox.

That's a different job than the old portal did. The portal's job was surfacing more than you'd ever click. The job now is holding the handful you already open every day, in the same place, so you stop hunting for them.

## Start page vs dashboard

That shift in what people actually want is exactly where "start page" stops being the right word for some of today's tools, TulipLot included.

A start page, by definition, is a place you leave. You land there when the browser opens, click through to wherever you're actually going, and its job is done until you close the browser fully and launch it again. Even the old portals worked this way underneath the widgets: useful for the first thirty seconds, then out of the picture.

A dashboard is a place you stay. TulipLot is built as a fixed 3×2 grid, six cells, each holding one app, and instead of a launch pad, it works more like a permanent workspace. Free accounts get five usable cells plus an ad cell in the corner; Premium is $4 a month for all six cells with no ads. Free needs no credit card and has no time limit either way. Add a site from the catalog or paste any HTTPS link, and drag two cells to swap them whenever your routine shifts. The grid stays exactly where you left it, tomorrow and the week after, because you're not passing through it. You're working inside it, same layout, same six spots, every day.

That's the real distinction, and it has nothing to do with widgets versus apps. A start page hands you a launch pad and steps aside. A dashboard doesn't step aside. We wrote more about that choice in [Why we built TulipLot](/blog/why-we-built-tuliplot), and if six fixed cells sounds like the wrong shape for how you compare things side by side, [how to view multiple websites at once](/blog/view-multiple-websites-at-once) covers the other ways people handle that instead.

## Do you still need one?

It depends entirely on your day, and it's worth answering honestly instead of assuming everyone needs the same setup.

If your actual routine is two sites, an inbox and one other tab, you don't need a start page, a dashboard, or anything layered on top of what your browser already does by default. Bookmark the two, or pin the tabs, and you're done. Adding a tool to manage two things solves a problem you don't have.

If you're checking five or six things all day, every day, and you keep catching yourself hunting through a pile of tabs to find the one you actually need, that's a different situation. A fixed layout, the same spot every time you look, beats re-finding the same handful of tabs over and over, day after day. At that point the apps aren't the problem. Where they live is.

[Try TulipLot free](/try), no credit card required, and see whether your five or six actually settle into a place that sticks.

## Questions

### What's the difference between a start page and a home page?

In Chrome and Edge, a start page loads when you launch the browser from fully closed, a cold start, controlled by the browser's startup setting, while a home page loads only when you click the dedicated Home button next to the address bar, a separate setting most people configure once and rarely revisit. Firefox is the exception: its single "Homepage and new windows" setting covers both, so there's no separate start-page setting to distinguish there. In Chrome and Edge, where the two settings are separate, they can still point at the same URL, which is part of why the terms get confused even though they're triggered by two different actions.

### Is there a modern replacement for iGoogle?

Not really, not as a direct swap. Nothing aggregates feeds and widgets onto a single page quite the way iGoogle did, because the model it was built for, RSS boxes and headline skimming, isn't how most people track things anymore. What replaced it wasn't one site; it was a wider shift toward checking dedicated apps directly. If what you actually miss is the "everything in one place" feeling rather than the feed format itself, a fixed dashboard like TulipLot is the closer modern equivalent, holding your real apps instead of summaries of them.

### Do I need an extension to use a start page?

No. Setting a start page is a native browser feature, built into every major browser's settings with no extension required. Some dashboard-style tools offer an optional extension for sites that actively resist being displayed inside another page, TulipLot's free Companion is one example, but that's a workaround for a specific slice of sites, not a requirement for using the tool at all.

# Five ways to lay out a productive dashboard
Source: https://tuliplot.com/blog/dashboard-productivity-tips/
Published: 2026-08-01

A fixed 3×2 grid only pays off if you arrange it around how you actually work. Six cells look the same empty, but a productive dashboard for someone glued to a support queue looks nothing like one for someone deep in a single project all day. The apps matter less than the dashboard layout: where each sits, what's asleep, and what earns the cell your eyes hit first. A grid isn't the only way to do this, either; if you're still weighing your options, [other ways to view multiple websites at once](/blog/view-multiple-websites-at-once) covers the rest.

Below are five layouts, each built for a different way of working. Pick whichever sounds like your day, or borrow pieces from two. Every layout fits a real 3×2 grid; one uses Premium's sixth cell, and says so.

## 1. The communicator

If your day runs on messages, build the grid around staying reachable without living inside any one app.

Top row, left to right: mail, calendar, team chat. Mail and calendar (Gmail, Outlook, or Google Calendar) open in their own tab the moment you click the cell. They're one-click launchers, not panes you stare into. Team chat depends on the tool; add it and the cell tells you within seconds how it behaves.

Bottom row: tasks, notes such as Notion, and a news source such as Hacker News. Notion and Hacker News need the TulipLot Companion first — install it once, then enable it for each site separately (Notion and Hacker News are two separate grants), and both load live from then on. Tasks can be whatever you already use.

That's six named apps, so this layout leans on [Premium's sixth cell](/guides/premium-vs-free). On the free plan, drop the news cell — mail, calendar, chat, tasks, and notes still fill five cells cleanly, with the ad sitting quietly in the sixth.

Who it suits: support, sales, management — any role where being reachable is most of the job.

## 2. The maker

If most of your day is spent creating — writing, designing, building — the grid should say so. One cell carries the weight of your actual work; everything else is support, and it should stay out of your way until you invite it in.

Top-left: mail (Gmail or Outlook), a one-click launcher you check between tasks, not during them. Top-center: your main work surface — a Trello board, which embeds live, or a Notion doc, which needs the Companion installed and enabled for that site. This is the cell you expand into focus mode when you're deep in it. Top-right: team chat, same as above.

Bottom-left: calendar (Google Calendar), another one-click launcher. Bottom-center: a reference doc or notes app for quick lookups without leaving the grid. Bottom-right: the free plan's ad cell, or a second reference app on Premium.

The trick is the sleep control, and it only applies where there's live content to quiet: if your chat tool loads live in its cell, put it to sleep while you work and wake it on breaks, instead of letting notifications pull you out mid-thought. Mail and calendar need no such treatment. As launcher cells, they're already quiet until you click in, with no live content to interrupt you.

Five named apps, so this one runs comfortably on free.

Who it suits: writers, designers, developers — anyone whose best hours need one thing in front of them and everything else held at arm's length.

## 3. The monitor

If your job is watching for change, the layout should be built for glancing, not reading. Nothing here needs your full attention every minute — just enough visibility that you notice when something shifts.

Top row: your three glance-first panes — a status page, an analytics tool, and a second dashboard or uptime monitor, each added as a custom URL. The cell tells you within seconds whether a given one loads live, needs the Companion, or opens in its own tab instead. Keep these along the top, the row your eyes cross most.

Bottom-left: a news source such as Hacker News, which needs the Companion before it embeds live. Bottom-center: your calendar (Google Calendar), a one-click launcher rather than a live pane. Bottom-right: the ad cell on free, or a sixth glance target on Premium.

None of these cells are where you do the work. When a number moves, expand that cell into focus mode, dig in, then hit Esc and you're back to glancing across all six.

Who it suits: on-call engineers, support leads — anyone whose job is noticing before it's a problem, not sitting inside one app all day.

## 4. The researcher

Research work rotates through sources around a few things that stay put — your notes chief among them. Layout around what's stable, not what's currently open.

Top-left and top-center: two reference sites side by side, added as custom URLs for comparing passages or data without alt-tabbing; each is upfront on add about whether it embeds live, needs the Companion, or opens in its own tab. Top-right: your notes — Notion works well here (install the Companion, enable it for the site, and it embeds live), or any notes app you prefer.

Bottom-left: a search engine or library database for pulling in new sources. Bottom-center: your calendar (Google Calendar), a one-click launcher for keeping research time on the schedule. Bottom-right: the free plan's ad cell, or a third reference site on Premium.

The move that makes this layout hold up over weeks: when a source stops being useful, don't delete the cell and rebuild — use edit to swap the new site into the same slot. The position stays fixed, so your notes cell stays exactly where it was relative to your sources, and you never lose the habit of reaching top-left for "current source A."

Who it suits: students, analysts — anyone whose sources change constantly but whose workflow shouldn't.

## 5. The minimalist

Not everyone wants six things running. If three apps cover your whole day, the other cells don't need to be empty — they need to be asleep.

Top row: your three actives. Mail and calendar (Gmail, Outlook, or Google Calendar) are one-click launchers that open in their own tab; the third slot holds one live app, such as a Trello board.

Bottom row: two more occasional apps — notes, a second chat, whatever earns a spot but not constant attention — added once and put to sleep. A slept cell stays exactly where you left it and shows nothing new until you wake it: not gone, just quiet.

Bottom-right is where the tiers differ. On free, that's the ad cell, and it was never going to hold one of your three actives anyway, so it stays out of the way. On Premium, it's a third sleeping cell — or leave it empty; an empty cell costs nothing.

Who it suits: anyone who tried a crowded grid and found it noisier than the tab wall it replaced.

## Placement rules that make any layout stick

A few rules cut across all five layouts, whichever one you start from.

**Top-left goes to whatever you check most.** Eyes land there first on every screen, every time, so give it to your highest-frequency check — inbox, chat, whatever pulls at you all day — not to whatever feels most important on paper.

**Group by how often you glance, not by app type.** A status page you check every few minutes doesn't belong next to a report you open once a week, even if both count as "analytics." Sort by rhythm first, category second.

**Sleep what you check hourly.** If a cell earns a glance every hour or two rather than constantly, put it to sleep between checks and wake it deliberately, instead of letting it refresh for no one.

**Expand what you work in, not what you watch.** Focus mode suits cells you're actively producing inside — a doc, a board, a ticket — not monitoring, which wants peripheral vision more than a full screen.

None of this is fixed forever. Drag two cells to swap them the moment your day changes shape, and the grid catches up instantly.

Layout is the cheapest lever you have. The apps barely change; where you put them changes how the day feels. Still deciding which five — or six — apps deserve a seat? [Getting started with TulipLot](/guides/getting-started) walks through the whole setup, cell controls included. Curious why we built a fixed grid instead of another tab manager? Read [Why we built TulipLot](/blog/why-we-built-tuliplot). And if you don't have a grid yet, [create a free account](/register) — no card required — and have one of these layouts running before your coffee's gone cold.

# Why we built TulipLot
Source: https://tuliplot.com/blog/why-we-built-tuliplot/
Published: 2026-08-01

## The tab pile: what too many browser tabs actually costs

You know the pile. It starts with a couple of tabs in the morning, and by the afternoon you've got too many browser tabs open at once — a wall of them, and somewhere in there is the doc you were editing earlier, except now it's drifted somewhere to the left of where you last saw it, next to another tab from the same site that you opened because you couldn't find the first one.

The favicons blur together after a while. You hover, wait for the tooltip, hover the next one, wait again. You've got a duplicate of the same dashboard open because you forgot you already had it. The tab you actually need is the one that always seems to have wandered off, and you spend stray moments, over and over, just relocating things you already opened once.

None of that is a discipline problem. Nobody fails at tabs. The browser tab bar was built to hold pages you're skimming for a minute and then closing, not the handful of apps you live inside all day, every day, for months on end. Ask it to be a home for your workflow and it's going to sag under the weight, no matter how careful you are about closing things.

## Why the usual fixes didn't stick for us

We tried the standard advice, same as you probably have. Tab groups color-code the pile into sections, which helps for about a day, until the sections themselves start multiplying and you're back to hunting, just within a smaller haystack. Tab managers and tree-style extensions impose more structure on top, but the structure lives inside the same bar, competing for the same sliver of horizontal space. It's still a pile. It's just a pile with labels.

Splitting apps across separate browser windows helps for exactly the apps you keep in view, and fragments everything else. Now you're alt-tabbing between windows instead of tabs, which is the same problem wearing a different hat. And more monitors don't solve it either, not really. A second or third screen just gives the pile more room to spread out. You still can't find the one tab you need, you can just fail to find it across a wider desk.

Every fix we tried treated the symptom. The tabs kept accumulating because nothing changed about where things lived.

## A fixed place for everything

So we stopped trying to organize the pile and got rid of it instead. TulipLot turns one browser tab into a 3×2 grid: six fixed cells, each holding one app, each cell staying exactly where you put it.

The bet is on spatial memory over search. You don't search for your keys every morning, because they live in the bowl by the door. Once you decide mail goes top-left, it stays top-left, tomorrow and the week after. You stop reading labels and start just reaching for where things are. Drag any two cells to swap them if your workflow changes, and the grid still stays fixed at six, so there's no fresh pile to manage in its place.

That's the whole trade. You give up the infinite, anything-goes tab bar for six spots you actually remember. For the handful of apps most of us live in daily, that's a fair trade to make.

## Built for the real web

Here's the part we won't dress up: a lot of the web doesn't want to be put in a box like this, and that's the site's call to make. Some sites send an explicit signal telling browsers not to frame them elsewhere, full stop. That's a real security choice by real teams, and when a site refuses outright like that, TulipLot isn't in the business of overriding it.

What we can do is be honest about which case you're in, cell by cell. Add a site and one of three things happens. Plenty of the catalog, and plenty of custom HTTPS URLs, just embed and load live right there in the grid. Some sites need a nudge: install the free TulipLot Companion extension once, then flip it on for that specific site, and the cell unlocks. It only touches the sites you explicitly enable, one at a time, and it isn't a bypass for everything. A handful of sites, Gmail and Google Calendar are the common examples, stay outside the grid no matter what you enable. The Companion doesn't change that. For those, the cell becomes a one-click launcher: click it, and the app opens in its own tab the way it always has.

We'd rather show you which of those three is true the moment you add a site than fake an embed that breaks the first time you click something inside it.

## What we deliberately left out

We left things out on purpose, and we want to say which, because the constraint is the actual point.

The grid is fixed at 3×2. No resizing panes, no dragging the borders wider, no seventh cell you unlock by rearranging harder. Six is the number.

There are no tabs inside a cell either. Each cell holds one app, not a stack of them. Opening a second tab inside a cell just rebuilds the pile you came here to leave, one cell at a time, and we're not interested in shipping that.

And there's no feed. No aggregated timeline pulling content from all six apps into one scroll. TulipLot shows you where your apps live. It doesn't try to read them for you.

Every one of those is a deliberate no, not a missing feature. A dashboard that does everything is just a tab bar with worse ergonomics.

## Where it's going

We're still early, and the roadmap gets shaped by what people actually run into, not by what looks good on a features page. If you want to see the grid in the shape other people have already found useful, we wrote up [five ways to lay out a productive dashboard](/blog/dashboard-productivity-tips) with real cell-by-cell examples.

If you've got five minutes, our [getting started guide](/guides/getting-started) walks the whole setup, first app to sixth cell. And if something about TulipLot doesn't fit the way you actually work, or you've got an idea for what should, we'd rather hear it than guess. Reach us through [About](/about).

Otherwise, the fastest way to see whether the fixed-grid bet pays off for you is to [try it with no account](/try): two live cells, no signup. Ready for the full grid? [Create a free account](/register), no credit card, and put your first five apps somewhere they'll actually stay.
